# Chapter Fourteen: The Captain's Chair

The Captain sat in the chair.

It was a heavy, oxblood leather armchair positioned squarely in the center of the subterranean command vault beneath the Order of Saint Francis's European operations hub. Across from Captain Thomas Mercer, three high-definition monitors glowed in the dim, recessed halogen light, displaying real-time orbital telemetry, satellite thermal mapping of the Mid-Atlantic seaboard, and high-resolution surveillance sweeps of eastern Scotland.

Mercer was a man carved from cold flint. In his late forties, with cropped iron-gray hair, a clean-shaven jaw, and a tailored black tactical uniform bearing the subtle embroidered red cross of the Custodes Sanguinis on the collar, he radiated the grim discipline of an inquisitor born into the digital age. He had not taken vows of poverty or pastoral gentleness. His vows were obedience, secrecy, and the merciless eradication of preternatural contaminants.

Beside him, Proctor Gregory tapped rapidly on an encrypted console. "Telemetry confirms the target package arrived at the Dundee safe site approximately sixteen hours ago, Captain. Father Edgar has secured the estate. Subject Victor Vance is inside the perimeter, undergoing stage-one assimilation."

Mercer leaned forward, resting his steepled fingers against his chin. "And the sword?"

"Secured in the armory vault alongside the Jamestown dagger. Edgar reports the initial neural resonance test was positive. The descendant handled the steel without rejection. In fact, he absorbed ten years of Alfonso's tactical muscle memory in less than four hours."

A thin, humorless smile touched Mercer's lips. "Then Ferdinand's blood is true. After seven centuries of hiding among mortal commoners, the royal sequence remains potent. That is convenient. A divine weapon without an ignition key is nothing more than ornamental iron."

"Bishop Talbot remains insistent that we proceed with pastoral caution, sir," Gregory noted, glancing nervously at a blinking red indicator on the communications console. "His Eminence believes Victor must be guided, not coerced. He views the descendant as an instrument of divine reconciliation."

"Talbot is an old theologian who smells of incense and dead parchment," Mercer replied coldly, his voice devoid of warmth. "He believes God intends for men and beasts to share this earth. He forgets the blood spilled on the plains of Castile, the massacres in the Black Forest, and the slaughtered settlers of the New World. You cannot reconcile with a cancer, Gregory. You excise it. We did not spend forty million dollars developing Project Argentum to broker peace treaties."

Mercer gestured at the right-hand monitor, which displayed schematic blueprints of a heavy industrial container rig fitted with pressurized aerosol distribution nozzles. "How soon until the aerosol dispersion unit is staged in the Highlands?"

"The transport arrived at the Aberdeen depot yesterday morning, disguised as agricultural machinery," Gregory reported. "Two hundred liters of weaponized micro-particulate silver, suspended in a volatile aerosol carrier. When deployed over the Glen Clova sanctuary, it will achieve ninety-nine percent atmospheric saturation within twenty minutes. Every creature carrying the active lycanthrope marker within a five-mile radius will suffer catastrophic cellular necrosis in under two minutes."

"And civilian collateral?" Mercer asked dispassionately.

"The glen is sparsely populated. A few isolated crofters and hill walkers. To mortal lungs, Argentum-9 produces nothing more than mild bronchial irritation—easily masked as an industrial chemical leak from the coast."

"Good," Mercer said, rising from his chair. "Let Talbot play his games with Victor in Dundee. Once the descendant's presence draws the rogue pack out of hiding, we deploy the payload. We wipe out the Scottish elders and the American rogues in a single stroke. And if the descendant perishes in the crossfire? The Church will canonize him as a holy martyr, and Lobera will return to our armory, where it belongs."

Meanwhile, three thousand miles across the Atlantic, the sun was just beginning to rise over the rolling fields of the Virginia horse country.

In the oak-paneled dining room of Isabella's secluded estate, Sowain—known to the mortal world centuries ago as Alfonso—sat across from Marcus, his enforcer. The morning light filtered through heavy velvet curtains, catching the silver streaks in Alfonso's dark beard and illuminating the deep scars running across his forearms. Though the herbal draught had forced his wounds to knit, the exhaustion of seven centuries of struggle weighed heavily in his dark, amber-flecked eyes.

Marcus leaned back in his chair, folding his arms. "I spoke to Patricia and Timothy. The bomb that took out our Rockville garage wasn't amateur work. It was military-grade C4 with an electronic radio trigger. Brock didn't just go rogue; he had outside backing."

"He didn't act alone," Alfonso agreed quietly, staring down at his weathered hands. "Martin has been whispering in his ear for months. Martin believes the ancient treaties are a collar around our necks. He believes that if they kill the last descendant and shatter Ferdinand's blade, the Order will lose its divine mandate and humanity will be ripe for the taking."

"Brock doesn't realize he's being played," Marcus growled. "The Order's strike teams don't make deals with wolves. If Martin and Brock think they can cut a deal with the hunters, they're walking into a slaughter."

Alfonso stood up, his towering seven-foot presence commanding immediate silence. "I know the Order better than anyone alive, Marcus. Three hundred years ago, in the forests of Jamestown, I wore their robes. I carried their daggers. I swore their secret oaths upon the holy cross. I hunted my own kind because the priests told me they were demons spawned from Lucifer's breath."

He turned to the window, watching the morning mist cling to the Virginia meadows. "It was only when I tracked a dying wolf back to her den—finding an injured mother shielding three starving children, speaking an ancient tongue that predated Latin by ten thousand years—that the scales fell from my eyes. They weren't demons. They were humanity's elder brothers. A forgotten genetic safeguard, blessed with the speed and tooth of the wild to protect early man from the true terrors of the primeval night."

Alfonso's voice dropped to a low, gravelly rasp. "When the Order commanded me to burn that den, I refused. I took the bite to save their line, and in doing so, I chose exile. I took the name Sowain, but the blood of Castile still remembers. Victor Vance is the child of my brother's lineage. He carries my blood, and right now, the butchers in Rome are training him to become their executioner."

"What do we do, Alpha?" Marcus asked, standing at attention.

Alfonso reached into his coat and produced three private passports and a set of chartered flight credentials. "Isabella has arranged a flight out of Dulles directly into Glasgow. Rebecca is already packing the gear. We are going to Scotland."

"To kill Brock?"

"To stop Brock," Alfonso corrected firmly. "And to make sure that young Victor Vance learns the truth before the Order turns him into a monster."
